title: Consensus (Raft)
subtitle: Watch five servers agree on one write, lose their leader, elect a new one, and never lose a committed entry.
learn: Why a group of machines needs consensus instead of one trusted copy
How Raft elects a leader using terms, randomized timeouts and majority votes
How log replication and majority commit make a write durable
Why a minority partition can never commit and a stale leader is forced to step down
What etcd and ZooKeeper use consensus for, and what they are not for

steps.title: Who decides what is true?
steps.body: You keep a cluster's critical settings, such as which node owns which job, on one server. That server dies and everything stops. So you keep copies on five servers. Now a harder problem appears: if two clients write different values at the same moment, or a server crashes mid-write, how do all five end up agreeing on one history? Making machines agree despite crashes and lost messages is called consensus.
steps.idea: Replication gives availability; consensus is what keeps the copies from disagreeing.
steps.caption: Five servers must act like one reliable machine.

steps.title: One leader, many followers
steps.body: Raft simplifies the problem by electing a single leader. Only the leader accepts writes. Followers copy what the leader sends and reply. Time is cut into numbered terms; each term has at most one leader, and the term number acts as a logical clock. Here S1 leads term 1 and sends tiny heartbeats, every 100 ms or so, to prove it is alive.
steps.idea: One leader per term means writes are ordered in one place, so there is nothing to argue about.
steps.caption: S1 leads term 1 and sends heartbeats.

steps.title: A write enters the log
steps.body: A client sends set x=5. The leader appends it to its own log, an ordered list of commands, and sends an AppendEntries message to every follower with the entry and its position. Each follower writes the entry to disk before answering. At this point the entry exists but is not yet committed, so the leader has not told the client anything.
steps.idea: A log entry is just a proposal until enough servers have stored it.
steps.caption: Leader appends x=5 and sends it to all followers.

steps.title: Majority means committed
steps.body: Followers reply as they finish their disk writes. The moment the leader plus two followers hold the entry, three of five, a majority has it. The entry is now committed: it will survive any failure the cluster is allowed to survive. The leader applies it, answers the client, and tells followers to apply it on the next message. In one data center this takes a few milliseconds, mostly the disk flush.
steps.idea: Commit means a majority has it on disk, so any future leader's majority must overlap and include it.
steps.caption: Three of five have it, so x=5 is committed.

steps.title: The leader dies
steps.body: Next S1 goes silent, whether from a crash or a long pause. Followers expect a heartbeat every 100 ms or so. When none arrives within the election timeout, each follower's election timer runs down and it becomes a candidate. The timeout is randomized per server (etcd defaults: 100 ms heartbeat, 1000 ms election timeout) so they do not all fire at the same instant. Until a new leader exists, the cluster accepts no writes: a write sent during this gap waits at least one election timeout, about a second with etcd defaults, before it can commit.
steps.idea: Followers detect a dead leader by silence; random timeouts make simultaneous candidates unlikely.
steps.caption: Heartbeats stop; S3's timer fires first.

steps.title: S3 asks for votes
steps.body: S3's timer fires first. It increments the term to 2, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote to the others. Each server grants at most one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. S2 and S4 say yes. With its own vote that makes three of five, a majority, so S3 becomes leader of term 2 and immediately sends heartbeats.
steps.idea: One vote per server per term guarantees at most one leader per term.
steps.caption: S3 wins term 2 with votes from S2 and S4.

steps.title: Committed entries survive
steps.body: Why is x=5 not lost? It sits on a majority, and any winning candidate also needs a majority of votes. Two majorities of five must share at least one server, and that server refuses to vote for a candidate missing x=5. So the new leader always holds every committed entry. If S1 had only been cut off or frozen (a long pause or a network blip) rather than crashed, it would still believe it leads term 1. Its first message from S3 carries term 2, so it steps down and its uncommitted entries are overwritten. A server that truly crashed simply restarts as a follower.
steps.idea: Quorum overlap plus the up-to-date vote rule means a committed entry can never be elected away.
steps.caption: Stale S1 sees term 2 and becomes a follower.

steps.title: A network partition
steps.body: Suppose a network split leaves S4 and S5 alone, cut off from the other three. S1 has rejoined as a follower, so S1, S2 and S3 form a majority of three and keep working with S3 as leader. S4 and S5 can reach only 2 of the 3 votes they would need, so they cannot elect a leader or commit anything. S4 may bump its own term to 3, but that term can never win. Real implementations add a pre-vote check so an isolated server does not inflate its term and disrupt the leader when the network heals. The minority refuses to answer rather than risk two conflicting histories, which is the consistency choice from the CAP lesson.
steps.idea: Only the side holding a majority may make progress, so a partition can never produce two committed histories.
steps.caption: S4 and S5 are isolated and cannot commit.

steps.title: What etcd and ZooKeeper do
steps.body: You rarely write Raft yourself. etcd (Raft) and ZooKeeper (a similar protocol called Zab) run a small cluster of 3 or 5 servers that stores a small, critical amount of data: configuration, who is leader of a service, cluster membership, locks. Kubernetes keeps all its state in etcd. These stores are slow for bulk data because every write pays a quorum round trip, so keep them for coordination, not for your application's rows.
steps.idea: Use consensus stores for small, high-value coordination state, and never as your main database.
steps.caption: A client reads and writes small coordination data.

steps.title: Agreement by majority
steps.body: Raft elects one leader per numbered term, replicates a log entry to followers, and commits it once a majority has stored it. A new leader needs a majority of votes, and those voters must hold every committed entry, so committed data survives leader crashes. Minorities stall instead of diverging. Pay for it with a quorum round trip per write, and use it for small coordination data.
steps.idea: Majority plus terms gives one history, at the cost of a quorum round trip per write and no progress without a majority.
steps.caption: Leader, terms, majority commit, safe failover.

quiz.q: A Raft cluster has 5 servers. The leader has stored an entry itself, and one follower has also stored it. Can the leader tell the client the write is committed?
options: Yes, two copies is enough to survive one crash
No, it needs at least 3 of 5 servers to hold the entry
Yes, because the leader's own copy is authoritative
No, it needs all 5 servers to hold the entry
quiz.why: Commit requires a majority, 3 of 5. With only 2 copies, the other three servers could form a majority, elect a leader without the entry, and the write would be lost.

quiz.q: Why must a server refuse to vote for a candidate whose log is behind its own?
options: To keep elections short
To stop the old leader from restarting
To prevent followers from voting twice in a term
To make sure the winner already holds every committed entry
quiz.why: Any committed entry sits on a majority, and any winning candidate also needs a majority of votes. The overlapping server blocks candidates that lack the entry.

quiz.q: A 6-server cluster is split into groups of 3 and 3 by a network failure. What happens?
options: Both groups elect leaders and keep accepting writes
The group containing the old leader keeps working
Neither group can reach a majority of 4, so neither can commit
The group with the lowest server IDs wins automatically
quiz.why: A majority of 6 is 4. With 3 and 3, neither side has it, so writes stall. This is also why odd cluster sizes are preferred.

quiz.q: The leader of term 1 was frozen by a long pause. Meanwhile S3 won term 2. When the old leader resumes, it still thinks it leads and tries to send an entry. What happens?
options: Followers reject it because its term is lower, and it steps down
Followers accept it if it has more entries than S3
Followers accept it because it arrived last
Followers start a new election in term 1
quiz.why: A paused or partitioned leader can still believe it leads. Servers reject messages from a lower term, and a leader that sees a higher term immediately becomes a follower. Terms keep stale leaders harmless.

quiz.q: Which workload is a poor fit for storing directly in etcd or ZooKeeper?
options: Service leader and membership info
A cluster's feature-flag configuration
Millions of per-user order rows with heavy write traffic
A distributed lock's ownership record
quiz.why: Every write goes through a single leader and waits for a quorum, and the whole dataset is replicated to each server. Coordination state is small, but bulk application data should live in a scalable database.

cheatsheet.def: Getting a group of machines to agree on one value or one ordered history even when some crash or messages are lost.
Numbered election period in Raft. At most one leader per term; a higher term always overrides a lower one.
More than half the servers: floor(N/2)+1. A cluster of 2f+1 servers survives f failures.
A leader may report an entry committed once a majority has stored it durably. Never earlier.
How long a follower waits without a heartbeat before running for leader. Randomized per server to avoid ties; must exceed the heartbeat interval by a wide margin.
A server only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so the winner has every committed entry.
Small, strongly consistent stores built on Raft (etcd) or Zab (ZooKeeper). Used for config, leader election, membership and locks, not bulk data.
Use 3 or 5 servers. Even sizes add cost without adding failure tolerance, and more servers make every write slower.
